paragraphs: This paper studies decisions that happen in two stages: choose how a system will operate, then decide whether to accept the request that arrives. Examples include choosing an LLM serving configuration or a fare class. The first decision changes the distribution of possible rewards and resource demands; the second uses the observed request to decide whether accepting it is worthwhile.

The authors show why evaluating this joint problem requires a benchmark that accounts for changing configurations over time. Their switching-aware fluid oracle includes the value of mixing configurations and provably upper-bounds what any online policy can achieve. They formulate its evaluation as a max-min problem and characterize its saddle points through conditions connecting feasibility, equilibrium, and complementary resource constraints.

These mathematical conditions guide SP-UCB–OLP, which selects decisions by solving an optimistic saddle-point problem. Its regret guarantee scales as roughly the square root of K times T, up to logarithmic factors, where K counts configurations and T counts periods. The result gives a theoretical performance guarantee for coordinating configuration choice with admission decisions.
icml-2026-a-two-layer-framework-for-join.tldr: A two-stage online algorithm coordinates configuration choices and request acceptance with a regret guarantee against a switching-aware benchmark.

paragraphs: This study asks whether artificial models and biological brains develop similar internal representations despite their different architectures and learning mechanisms. The authors compare 630 language and vision models, spanning 1.33 million to 72 billion parameters, with brain activity measured by fMRI in the Natural Scenes Dataset. Their analysis produces more than 60 million alignment measurements.

Within each modality, better-performing models tend to show stronger correspondence with brain activity. The reported correlations are 0.89 for language models and 0.53 for vision models. Because the brain responses were evoked by images, the language-model result concerns visual-semantic correspondence; it is not a direct comparison of language and vision processing under equivalent inputs.

Tracking training over time, the authors find that earlier brain alignment predicts later performance more reliably than the reverse in bidirectional Granger tests. This identifies alignment as an early correlate of learning, without establishing that it causes improvement. The regional patterns also differ: language models correspond more with limbic and integrative regions, while vision models align with visual cortical hierarchies.
icml-2026-alignment-between-brains-and-a.tldr: Across 630 AI models, stronger performance correlates with greater brain alignment, which also emerges as an early predictor of learning progress.

paragraphs: Correct code can still consume too much time or memory. BEST evaluates both dimensions of efficiency in code generated by language models, addressing the limited attention paid to memory use in earlier benchmarks. It contains 440 expert-constructed coding tasks, making resource efficiency an explicit part of the evaluation rather than treating correctness as the whole outcome.

Each task is divided into subtasks with different input sizes and difficulties. Experts provide a reference implementation for every subtask, described as Pareto-optimal: its time and space trade-off cannot be improved in one dimension without sacrificing the other. This finer evaluation distinguishes performance across input conditions instead of assigning one undifferentiated efficiency judgment to an entire task.

The authors also introduce dual@k, a metric that extends pass@k to account for both time and space through a weighting scheme over subtasks. Their evaluation of 50 language models finds weak time-efficient code generation and still weaker space-efficient generation. The findings show why evaluating both resources can expose shortcomings that correctness or runtime alone would leave unmeasured.
icml-2026-best-benchmarking-efficiency-i.tldr: BEST evaluates generated code on runtime and memory use, finding that 50 tested language models struggle especially with space efficiency.

paragraphs: CORE approaches manipulated multimodal content by looking for inconsistencies in what it communicates. These can be semantic or physical conflicts between modalities, or contradictions with common world knowledge. The motivation is that detectors trained around particular manipulation techniques can struggle when new techniques appear, especially when they depend on large amounts of labeled data.

The authors construct a Conflict Attribution Corpus with detailed annotations describing conflict factors and their sources. They use this corpus to strengthen the representations and reasoning of multimodal language models so that conflict detection becomes an explicit learned capability. This gives the model a common reasoning target across different kinds of manipulation.

Experiments report accuracy improvements over state-of-the-art models of 9.7%, 14.1%, and 11.8% on DGM⁴, MMFakeBench, and MDSM, respectively. CORE also adapts to unseen manipulation types with few examples or in zero-shot settings. These results support the usefulness of conflict-focused supervision for generalization, with the reported benefits tied to the evaluated benchmarks and adaptation settings.
icml-2026-core-conflict-oriented-reasoni.tldr: CORE trains multimodal models to identify inconsistencies, improving manipulation detection and adaptation to unseen manipulation types.

paragraphs: Some prediction systems have access during training to measurements that will be too expensive or slow to obtain at deployment. A common solution trains a model with this extra information, then uses its predictions on unlabeled examples to teach a deployable model. The paper examines a weakness of this sequence: weak or noisy extra information can produce misleading teaching signals and reduce accuracy.

The proposed method trains the two models jointly. This coupling lets learning account for the deployable model while using the additional training information, instead of passing predictions from a separately trained model in a fixed second stage. The intended benefit is to use the extra information when it helps without automatically inheriting its mistakes.

The authors provide guarantees describing conditions under which joint training improves prediction accuracy and analyze an alternating training algorithm for large, high-dimensional models. Experiments on synthetic data and medical prediction tasks show that the approach avoids the identified failures and consistently beats standard two-step baselines. The theoretical improvement remains conditional on the circumstances covered by those guarantees.
icml-2026-coupled-training-with-privileg.tldr: Jointly training privileged-information and deployable models improves how extra training-only information is used, avoiding failures observed with two-step teaching.

paragraphs: Recovering training examples from a trained network raises two separate questions: whether the available equations uniquely specify the data, and whether an optimization procedure can actually find them. This paper studies both questions for reconstruction methods that use Karush–Kuhn–Tucker, or KKT, conditions, which describe mathematical relationships associated with an optimization solution.

For two-layer networks with polynomial activation functions, the authors discuss sufficient conditions under which the KKT equations uniquely determine the training data. These conditions help explain when reconstruction is identifiable. Their sufficiency matters: the result establishes circumstances that permit uniqueness, rather than claiming that reconstruction requires those conditions in every case.

To improve recovery in practice, the authors introduce sample splitting as a refinement step that uses the curvature of the reconstruction objective. It creates additional directions in which the objective can decrease, helping escape poor stationary points and improve candidate reconstructions. The step applies beyond KKT-based objectives. Experiments show consistent reconstruction improvements when sample splitting is added to several existing methods, connecting the theoretical question of uniqueness with the practical challenge of finding good solutions.
icml-2026-data-reconstruction-identifiab.tldr: The paper studies when training data are uniquely recoverable and introduces a curvature-aware refinement that improves existing reconstruction methods.

paragraphs: This paper develops vision-language pretraining for three-dimensional CT scans using radiology reports as supervision. It addresses two problems: processing volumetric images efficiently and matching their visual information to disease-specific meanings in reports. Its hybrid encoder replaces a vision transformer's patch embedding with a 3D convolutional backbone, combining local anatomical detail with global attention and compatibility with pretrained cross-modal knowledge.

The training objective uses learnable query tokens to extract disease-specific information from full reports and align it with corresponding image features. This aims to separate diseases that occur within the same anatomical region. A diagnosis-aware prompting strategy then combines real clinical phrases with aggregated disease prototypes to better connect pretraining with zero-shot diagnosis.

The model reports state-of-the-art AUC results of 84.4% on CT-RATE and 75.4% on Rad-ChestCT, with stated gains of 5.1% and 5.4%. It reports a larger 9.8% AUC gain on a 60-disease benchmark and strong transfer to report generation. Together, the results support the value of combining efficient volumetric encoding with more precise disease-level alignment.
icml-2026-disease-centric-vision-languag.tldr: A hybrid CT encoder and disease-specific report alignment improve zero-shot diagnostic performance and transfer to radiology report generation.

paragraphs: Heima addresses the cost of generating long textual reasoning chains in multimodal language models. It compresses these chains into a small collection of abstract thinking tokens, aiming to retain useful reasoning information while removing redundant expression. This changes how intermediate reasoning is represented, reducing the need to spell out every step in a lengthy text sequence.

The authors analyze compression through information theory, quantifying the information gap it introduces. Their analysis states that reasoning capability is preserved when non-trivial mutual information remains. That condition is central to the claim: compression must retain relevant information rather than merely shorten the representation. An adaptive interpreter maps the thinking tokens back into text sequences of variable length to examine what they preserve.

Across reasoning benchmarks, Heima improves efficiency while maintaining or sometimes improving zero-shot accuracy. The interpreter also reconstructs coherent reasoning from the compressed tokens, which the authors interpret as evidence of a minimal information gap. These findings support compact internal reasoning representations and provide a way to inspect the reasoning information they retain.
icml-2026-efficient-reasoning-with-hidde.tldr: Heima compresses multimodal reasoning into abstract thinking tokens, improving efficiency while retaining or improving tested zero-shot accuracy.

paragraphs: A classifier can predict labels accurately while assigning confidence values that do not reliably reflect its correctness. This paper proposes a unified calibration framework for arbitrary distribution-based classifiers. Its aim is to connect a mathematically specified form of individual calibration with reliable classifier behavior, while keeping the method usable within practical neural-network training.

The calibration objective guarantees a monotone Probably Approximately Individually Calibrated predictor, abbreviated mPAIC. The authors show that this property implies Probably Approximately Calibrated Classifier guarantees with explicit error bounds. The probabilistic and approximate qualifications are part of the result: the framework supplies bounded calibration claims rather than asserting perfect confidence estimates for every prediction.

For optimization, Decoupled Dual-Stream Optimization uses gradient detachment to reconcile learning discriminative representations with continuous calibration. The framework can serve either as an end-to-end training objective or as a lightweight adapter applied after training. Across nine real-world datasets, the authors report improvements over strong baselines in both accuracy and calibration at multiple levels, supporting the framework's practical use alongside its theoretical guarantees.
icml-2026-from-individual-calibration-to.tldr: A calibration framework links individual-level guarantees to classifier reliability and improves accuracy and calibration across nine datasets.

paragraphs: Gradient clipping limits unusually large updates during stochastic optimization. Its theoretical motivation often involves heavy-tailed noise whose variance may be infinite, yet every empirical moment is finite for a fixed finite dataset. This paper resolves that apparent contradiction by separating randomness in drawing the dataset from randomness in selecting examples during optimization.

Although the noise variance is finite after fixing a dataset, its magnitude can grow as the dataset becomes larger. When gradient norms at the population minimizer have tail index alpha between one and two, the empirical average of squared norms scales as N to the power 2/alpha minus one. This growth weakens standard SGD convergence guarantees as sample size N increases.

The authors show that clipped SGD avoids this growth and establish finite-sum convergence guarantees for broad choices of step sizes and clipping schedules. They also derive generalization bounds for strongly convex, smooth objectives. The analysis identifies gradient tails at the population minimizer as the key connection between optimization and generalization, with the generalization result specifically grounded in those objective assumptions.
icml-2026-from-optimization-to-generaliz.tldr: Separating data randomness from optimization randomness explains why gradient clipping improves theoretical guarantees under heavy-tailed data.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether language models can be trained to describe their own learned behaviors faithfully. A major obstacle is obtaining reliable labels for what a model has learned. The authors create such labels by fine-tuning copies of a target model with deliberately implanted behaviors, producing pairs of models and known behavioral descriptions.

They then jointly train a LoRA introspection adapter across these modified models so that each verbalizes its implanted behavior. The adapter also induces faithful reports in other fine-tunes trained through substantially different procedures and in the original target model itself. Transfer to the original model is especially notable because the adapter was never trained on that model directly.

The authors demonstrate applications by auditing previously introduced misaligned models and detecting fine-tuning API attacks involving encrypted harmful requests. They also find that adapters work better on larger models. These results suggest that deliberately constructed behavioral labels can support scalable introspection training, with demonstrated transfer beyond the models used to train the adapter and practical value for the reported auditing tasks.
icml-2026-introspection-adapters-trainin.tldr: Adapters trained on deliberately implanted behaviors help language models describe learned behaviors and support audits of misaligned models.

paragraphs: LaTtE-Flow targets models that both understand images and generate them. Such unified systems can require extensive pretraining and slow image generation, limiting their usefulness when time or resources are constrained. The proposed architecture starts with a pretrained vision-language model, retaining its multimodal understanding capabilities while adding an efficient flow-based image-generation mechanism.

The central design assigns different groups of transformer layers to different subsets of generation timesteps. At each sampling step, only a small group of layers is active, reducing the work required for that step. A timestep-conditioned residual attention mechanism additionally supports efficient reuse of information across layers. Together, these components make layer computation depend on where the model is in the generation process.

Experiments report strong multimodal understanding performance and competitive image-generation quality, alongside approximately sixfold faster inference than recent unified multimodal models. The result shows that specializing layer groups by timestep can improve sampling efficiency while retaining both capabilities within one framework. The speed claim is a comparison with the evaluated unified models, rather than a universal acceleration factor.
icml-2026-latte-flow-layerwise-timestep-.tldr: LaTtE-Flow activates specialized layer groups at different generation timesteps, achieving competitive image quality with approximately sixfold faster inference.

paragraphs: This paper learns which variables are conditionally related in a sparse Gaussian graphical model from one temporally dependent sequence of observations. Specifically, the sequence follows Glauber dynamics. This setting matters because observations in applications may arrive as a correlated trajectory, rather than as independent samples, and their dependence changes what a learning algorithm can exploit.

The algorithm first estimates conditional variances and rescales the observations so the problem has a unit diagonal, while preserving the underlying graph. It then examines short windows of updates to isolate the influence of one variable on another. These local edge tests extract adjacency information directly from the dynamics of the observed sequence.

A robust median-based estimator combines the local statistics, with a proof of accuracy despite contamination and temporal dependence. The authors establish polynomial-time graph recovery with a trajectory-length guarantee that does not depend on mixing time, the time needed for the dynamics to approach equilibrium. This provides a way to recover structure without making the required observation length depend on that equilibration timescale.
icml-2026-learning-gaussian-graphical-mo.tldr: A polynomial-time algorithm recovers sparse Gaussian graph structure from one Glauber trajectory with an observation-length guarantee independent of mixing time.

paragraphs: OmniVL-Guard addresses forgery detection in content that interleaves text, images, and videos. Its task includes both deciding whether content is authentic and locating the manipulated material. Combining these demands creates a training problem: learning a broad authenticity judgment and learning precise localization do not necessarily progress at the same rate.

The authors identify a difficulty bias in joint optimization. The easier classification task tends to dominate gradient updates, leaving fine-grained grounding underdeveloped. They first synthesize reasoning paths through a self-evolving chain-of-thought generation pipeline to support the initial training stage. They then introduce Adaptive Reward Scaling Policy Optimization, or ARSPO, to adjust reward scales and task weights dynamically.

By changing the training balance, ARSPO gives greater priority to the challenging grounding objectives while continuing to optimize detection. Experiments report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods and robust zero-shot generalization to out-of-domain scenarios. The findings connect better unified forgery analysis with explicitly managing the imbalance between deciding that something is manipulated and identifying where the manipulation occurs.
icml-2026-omnivl-guard-towards-unified-v.tldr: OmniVL-Guard balances authenticity classification and manipulation localization to improve forgery analysis across interleaved text, images, and videos.

paragraphs: Goal-oriented navigation requires a robot to find a specified target in an environment it has not fully explored. Map-based approaches must build a spatial representation while also estimating where an unseen goal might be. This paper introduces PLMD, a diffusion-based method that completes missing parts of a bird's-eye-view map with predicted obstacle and semantic labels.

The method generates labels for unobserved regions through a denoising diffusion process. It uses structural consistency between known and unknown obstacle layouts, then incorporates obstacle priors into semantic denoising. This connects predictions about what occupies a location with predictions about the surrounding physical layout, addressing inconsistent semantic associations in partially observed maps.

The completed labels support goal localization before the entire environment has been observed. Experiments show that PLMD extends maps into unknown regions, integrates into existing navigation strategies that use semantic maps, and achieves state-of-the-art performance on three goal-oriented navigation tasks. Its plug-and-play contribution is therefore a map-completion component that supplies existing navigation systems with useful predictions about unseen space.
icml-2026-plug-and-play-label-map-diffus.tldr: PLMD predicts obstacle and semantic labels in unseen map regions, helping existing navigation systems locate goals in partially explored environments.

paragraphs: Retrieval systems often use a fast embedding search to select candidates, then apply a more expensive model to rank them accurately. This saves computation, but the initial embedding stage can lose relevance information. The paper investigates how scores from the expensive ranking model can improve the query and item representations used for candidate selection.

Its central idea represents a query through its relevance to a collection of support items, and represents an item through its relevance to support queries. These relevance profiles are then used to obtain embeddings. The support collections provide reference points through which the richer ranking model informs the lightweight representations, making their selection an important part of the method.

The authors prove that embeddings constructed this way can approximate any complex similarity model under mild conditions. This is a conditional expressiveness result, rather than an unconditional guarantee for every support set. Experiments on diverse academic and production datasets illustrate the approach's effectiveness. Together, the results motivate using expensive relevance judgments to strengthen the earlier candidate-retrieval stage.
icml-2026-relevance-based-embeddings-lig.tldr: Relevance profiles against support queries and items turn expensive ranking scores into embeddings for lightweight candidate retrieval.

paragraphs: Scientific agents need to coordinate specialized tools across multiple steps, yet this ability is not well covered by existing benchmarks. SciAgentGym provides an interactive execution environment with 1,780 domain-specific tools across four natural science disciplines. Its companion evaluation suite, SciAgentBench, ranges from elementary actions to long workflows, allowing evaluation at different levels of coordination difficulty.

The evaluation finds that state-of-the-art models struggle with complex scientific tool use and deteriorate substantially as interactions become longer. To address this problem, the authors introduce SciForge, a training-data synthesis method that represents the tool action space as a dependency graph. It uses those dependencies to construct training trajectories that reflect the logical relationships among tool actions.

Fine-tuning on these trajectories produces SciAgent-8B, which outperforms the much larger Qwen3-VL-235B-Instruct in the reported evaluation. The model also exhibits positive transfer of scientific tool-use capabilities across domains. The results suggest that training on logically structured action sequences can improve scientific workflow execution, alongside providing an environment for measuring the remaining long-horizon challenge.
icml-2026-sciagentgym-benchmarking-multi.tldr: SciAgentGym exposes difficulties in long scientific tool workflows, while dependency-aware synthetic training improves an 8B agent's performance.

paragraphs: Continual learning asks a model to acquire new skills or knowledge while preserving what it already knows. Standard supervised fine-tuning learns from expert demonstrations, but its training examples are off-policy: they do not come from the model's current behavior. On-policy reinforcement learning can reduce forgetting, yet it depends on explicit rewards that may be unavailable.

Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning offers a way to obtain on-policy learning signals directly from demonstrations. The model uses its in-context learning ability to act as its own teacher when conditioned on a demonstration. This demonstration-conditioned teacher supplies signals for learning from the model's own behavior, connecting example-based instruction with an on-policy training approach.

Across skill-learning and knowledge-acquisition tasks, SDFT achieves higher new-task accuracy than supervised fine-tuning while substantially reducing catastrophic forgetting. In sequential experiments, one model accumulates multiple skills without performance regression. These findings support self-distillation as a practical approach to continual learning from demonstrations, with the no-regression result referring to the sequential settings tested in the paper.
icml-2026-self-distillation-enables-cont.tldr: Self-distillation uses demonstration-conditioned teaching to improve new-task learning while reducing forgetting compared with supervised fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Aligning a language model involves several objectives that can conflict, including objectively checkable outcomes, subjective preferences, and goals within interactive exchanges. Combining all these signals into one score can make training inefficient and limit users' ability to adjust priorities later. MAHALO provides a unified framework for retaining and coordinating multiple objectives across these settings.

The framework standardizes training for process reward models, which provide supervision at individual steps. It combines this with Multi-Action-Head Direct Preference Optimization to perform vectorized multi-objective alignment. During inference, objective-specific weights and process-reward-guided decoding let the system adjust how different goals influence its output. This connects the training objectives with controls available when the model is used.

Experiments cover mathematical reasoning, human-values alignment, and multi-turn tutoring. MAHALO improves multiple objectives simultaneously with limited interference and demonstrates generalization and adaptability across domains. The findings indicate that heterogeneous reward signals can be coordinated while preserving flexible inference-time control; they do not imply that all conflicts between objectives disappear.
icml-2026-simultaneous-multi-objective-a.tldr: MAHALO coordinates verifiable and subjective alignment objectives while allowing users to adjust objective priorities during inference.

paragraphs: Multimodal reasoning can accumulate long sequences of textual and visual intermediate steps, increasing computation and memory demands. SpecFlow replaces an expanding collection of visual thoughts with a fixed-size workspace represented in discrete cosine space. This representation concentrates information so that global layout and relationships can be retained while finer spatial details are introduced when needed.

Autoregressive textual thoughts steer flow-based updates of the visual workspace through classifier-free guidance. Each visual update depends on the current visual state and the accumulated textual trace, rather than adding more visual tokens to the context. The design therefore preserves a bounded visual workspace while allowing its contents to evolve with the reasoning process.

The paper reports stable latency and memory usage independent of reasoning depth for its framework, alongside competitive or superior reasoning performance in experiments. Computation and memory costs fall by up to a factor of 2.1. The findings support progressively refining a compact visual representation as a way to sustain longer multimodal reasoning without continually expanding its visual workspace.
icml-2026-spectral-progressive-thought-f.tldr: SpecFlow progressively updates a fixed-size visual reasoning workspace, reducing computation and memory costs by up to 2.1 times.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models generate text by repeatedly filling masked positions. Predicting many positions together can accelerate generation, but quality suffers when tokens that depend on one another are grouped into the same step. SPEED addresses this grouping problem through complementary changes to training and decoding, aiming to enlarge the sets of tokens that can safely be generated in parallel.

During training, the student learns from positions where the teacher is correct, using a temperature-scaled distribution-matching loss alongside masked language modeling. This concentrates more probability on correct token identities and brings more positions above the decoding threshold. During inference, Slow-Fast Decoding compares each token's predictions with and without the preceding block to estimate sensitivity to revealed context.

Low-sensitivity tokens are decoded together, while sensitive tokens wait for additional context. Experiments report speedups of up to 12.2 times on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and 6.7 times on Dream-7B-Instruct, with accuracy close to greedy decoding on reasoning and code benchmarks. The result ties acceleration to more selective parallel grouping, with the stated speedups representing the best reported cases.
icml-2026-speed-sharpened-teacher-distil.tldr: SPEED combines selective teacher distillation with context-sensitive token grouping to accelerate diffusion decoding while keeping accuracy close to greedy decoding.

paragraphs: Software engineering agents can store past problem-solving experience to help with future work. This paper finds that storing and retrieving whole episodes creates a mismatch: two tasks may sound similar overall while requiring different reasoning at particular stages. Retrieving an entire superficially similar episode can therefore guide an agent toward the wrong reasoning for its current subtask.

Structurally Aligned Subtask-Level Memory organizes storage, retrieval, and updates around the agent's functional decomposition. The unit of remembered experience follows the structure of the work being performed. This makes the memory mechanism more closely match the stage-specific reasoning needs that whole-episode retrieval can overlook, especially during long problem-solving sequences.

On SWE-bench Verified, the method consistently outperforms agents without the memory mechanism and strong instance-level memory baselines across multiple model backbones. Mean Pass@1 improves over the vanilla agent by 4.7 percentage points on average, including 6.8 points for Gemini 2.5 Pro. Gains grow with more interaction steps, supporting the value of appropriately organized past experience for longer software engineering tasks.
icml-2026-structurally-aligned-subtask-l.tldr: Organizing agent memory around subtasks improves software engineering performance, with larger gains during longer interactions.

paragraphs: This paper studies how the wording of training instructions affects fine-tuning. Semantically equivalent prompts often produce similar performance on the task being learned, yet the authors find that their effects on other tasks can differ sharply. Those differences include how much previous knowledge is forgotten and how well the resulting model generalizes.

The cross-task effects are positively correlated, indicating that some prompts consistently produce better outcomes across tasks. The authors further find that task loss measured before learning can robustly identify these superior prompts. This gives a signal for selecting training formulations based on the model's current state, rather than assuming that interchangeable wording leads to interchangeable learning.

State-Adaptive Prompt Optimization turns that finding into a lightweight training strategy, making task formulation a dynamic variable during fine-tuning. Across diverse benchmarks, it significantly reduces forgetting and improves generalization, with substantial reported gains over state-of-the-art methods. The results show that training prompts influence learning dynamics beyond immediate task accuracy and can serve as a practical control for more robust fine-tuning.
icml-2026-training-prompt-matters-state-.tldr: SAPO adapts training prompts to the model's state, using pre-learning task loss to help reduce forgetting and improve generalization.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks can save energy on neuromorphic hardware, but larger and deeper models can erode that advantage. UniSparse aims to improve efficiency by reducing both neuronal firing and network weights. It brings these two forms of sparsification into one framework so that they can contribute to a shared accuracy–energy trade-off.

The method builds on the finding that affine parameters in batch normalization also act as learnable thresholds for the spiking neurons that follow. Constraining those parameters reduces firing rates. A complementary weight-pruning method uses the same energy constraint, allowing it to integrate naturally with spike sparsification. The shared constraint connects fewer active signals with fewer retained weights.

Across models and datasets, the authors report a state-of-the-art balance between accuracy and energy efficiency. One sparsified ResNet-18 reaches 92.38% accuracy on CIFAR-10 using 7.04 million synaptic operations per inference. This result illustrates the combined method's efficiency at a stated accuracy level, while the broader energy motivation concerns deployment of spiking networks on neuromorphic hardware.
icml-2026-unisparse-combining-weight-pru.tldr: UniSparse jointly reduces spike activity and prunes weights to improve the accuracy–energy trade-off of spiking neural networks.

paragraphs: Processing long inputs in chunks lets a language model maintain a textual memory instead of handling everything at once. The paper identifies two weaknesses in MemAgent's recurrent approach: memory can grow through indiscriminate updates on chunks without useful evidence, and processing can continue even after sufficient evidence has been gathered. Both behaviors create unnecessary work.

GRU-Mem adds two text-controlled gates to this loop. An update gate determines whether the current chunk should change memory, while an exit gate determines whether processing should stop immediately. End-to-end reinforcement learning uses separate reward signals for correct updating and correct exiting, teaching the model to control both information retention and the duration of its reading process.

Experiments on multiple long-context reasoning tasks show improved effectiveness and efficiency, generally outperforming vanilla MemAgent and reporting substantial inference acceleration. The contribution is a learned decision about when further reading or memory revision is useful. This links long-context reasoning quality with explicit control over memory growth and computation, rather than updating and continuing at every chunk automatically.
icml-2026-when-to-memorize-and-when-to-s.tldr: GRU-Mem learns when to update textual memory and when to stop reading, improving long-context reasoning efficiency and performance.
